unit.name: Hype filtering and problem-first AI advising
unit.description: The lecture connects social-media hype, trusted advising, and concrete business problem decomposition, using an agent request as the core case.
unit.summary: Laurence says the currency of social media is engagement rather than accuracy, so AI practitioners need to filter signal from noise [ts=3425s]. In interviews or jobs, bringing signal rather than hype makes someone valuable as a trusted advisor [ts=3464s]. His agent story shows the problem-first method: when a company asks for an agent, start with 'why' and peel the request back to the real business goal [ts=3541s]. The eventual goal was to make salespeople more efficient, which does not inherently require an agent or even AI; the advisor must diagnose the actual task before selecting technology [ts=3603s].

key_points.text: Social-media platforms reward engagement, not accuracy, which distorts AI trend perception.
Filtering signal from noise is presented as a way to become distinctive and valuable.
When asked to implement an agent, the most fundamental first question is 'why?'.
The real business goal in the agent example was improving salesperson efficiency, not adopting AI for its own sake.
Text-to-video is decomposed into successive frame prediction to make the technology less magical and more reasoned about.

kp_catalog.name: Hype filtering and trusted advising
kp_catalog.description: High-value AI practitioners separate real signal from social-media hype and advise organizations around actual business needs.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Laurence warns that social media rewards engagement rather than accuracy and says signal filtering makes candidates and employees more valuable [ts=3425s].

kp_catalog.name: Problem-first AI solution design
kp_catalog.description: Effective AI advising starts from the underlying business problem rather than from a fashionable technology label such as agents.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Problem-first solution design is career/product judgment, useful but not a core DL prerequisite.
